title: Among boys and young men, loneliness is widespread but usually intermittent; family support, friendships, mental health, bullying and work or education status structure who becomes persistently disconnected
source_unit: UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport and National Centre for Social Research, Loneliness, isolation and social connection among boys and young men in England
geography: England; boys and young men aged 10–25 using Understanding Society and Mental Health of Children and Young People survey data

observations.period: 2022–2025; levels of loneliness among boys and young men

denominator.unit: two national survey frames: Understanding Society waves 14–15 and MHCYP wave 4

understanding_society_often.unit: percent of young men aged 16–25 reporting feeling lonely often in Understanding Society

understanding_society_some.unit: percent of boys and young men reporting feeling lonely some of the time in Understanding Society

mhcyp_often_always.unit: percent of boys and young men aged 11–25 reporting feeling lonely often or always in MHCYP

mhcyp_occasionally_some.unit: percent of boys and young men aged 11–25 reporting feeling lonely occasionally or some of the time in MHCYP

observations.method: Secondary analysis of Understanding Society waves 14 and 15 collected 2022–2025 and MHCYP wave 4 collected in 2023; survey questions differ and are comparable only at a broad level.
observations.uncertainty: The surveys use different age bands, wording and response options; percentages should not be treated as a single pooled prevalence estimate.
observations.subgroup: Boys aged 10–15 and young men aged 16–25 in England.
observations.counterinterpretation: Most respondents do not report chronic loneliness, but intermittent loneliness can still affect wellbeing, participation and help-seeking, especially when stigma suppresses disclosure.

observations.period: 2022–2025; isolation, support and friendship among young men

denominator.unit: young men aged 16–21 in England in the Understanding Society Wave 15 analysis of loneliness, isolation and friendship

isolation_often.unit: percent of young men aged 16–25 reporting feeling isolated often

isolation_some.unit: percent reporting feeling isolated some of the time

loneliness_small_friend_group.unit: percent of young men with no close friends reporting feeling lonely often, compared with approximately 9–11% among those with three or more friends

family_support_gap.unit: percent of young men with lower family support reporting loneliness often, compared with 10% among those with stronger family support

observations.method: Understanding Society Wave 15 descriptive and multivariable analysis of close friends, family support, loneliness and isolation.
observations.uncertainty: Associations may reflect mental health, bullying, socioeconomic conditions, family relationships and selection; friendship count is an imperfect proxy for meaningful connection.
observations.subgroup: Young men aged 16–21, with comparisons by close-friend group and perceived family support.
observations.counterinterpretation: More friends or family support may be outcomes of wellbeing and opportunity rather than independent interventions; quality and safety of relationships matter more than counts alone.

observations.period: 2022–2025; mental health, bullying and economic inactivity

denominator.unit: NatCen analysis of boys and young men aged 10–25 across two national surveys

mental_health.value: lower wellbeing, emotional difficulties and peer-relationship problems were the strongest and most consistent factors associated with loneliness and isolation

bullying.value: online or school bullying was closely associated with higher loneliness

economic_inactivity.value: unemployment or being economically inactive was associated with greater loneliness or isolation among young men, though some patterns weakened after accounting for wellbeing and bullying

causal_boundary.value: the report explicitly states that these associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships

observations.method: Secondary analysis of Understanding Society and MHCYP with descriptive and regression-based associations across personal, social, mental-health and socioeconomic factors.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional or observational associations cannot establish directionality; loneliness may both result from and contribute to mental-health, education, employment and relationship difficulties.
observations.subgroup: Boys and young men with poor wellbeing, peer difficulties, bullying exposure, unemployment or limited education and work connection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Employment or education may provide social connection for some young people, but can also be stressful or exclusionary; programme design must address quality and belonging, not only attendance.

denominator.unit: young men aged 16–21 in the Understanding Society Wave 15 analysis of in-person contact and social connection

daily_contact.unit: percent reporting chronic loneliness among young men meeting friends daily or several times a week

less_than_weekly_contact.unit: percent reporting chronic loneliness among young men meeting friends less often than once a week

isolation_daily_contact.unit: percent reporting frequent isolation among young men meeting friends almost every day

isolation_less_contact.unit: percent reporting frequent isolation among young men meeting friends less than once a week

organized_activity.value: participation in clubs, societies and community groups was associated with lower loneliness among some young men

observations.method: Understanding Society Wave 15 analysis of friendship-meeting frequency and MHCYP analysis of organised activity.
observations.uncertainty: Contact frequency is not equivalent to meaningful connection and may be confounded by mental health, transport, money, family support, school and work schedules; the evidence is associational.
observations.subgroup: Young men aged 16–21 and boys and young men participating or not participating in organized activities.
observations.counterinterpretation: More in-person contact may be a marker of existing wellbeing and resources; forced or low-quality contact may not reduce loneliness.

related_sources.claim: Official technical appendix and model details.
Policy framework that uses this empirical report.

boundary: This record is the empirical companion to the UK Social Connection Framework. It uses observational national survey data, with different measures across Understanding Society and MHCYP; it is not a causal intervention evaluation, clinical diagnosis, global estimate or proof that friendship counts alone create wellbeing.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official DCMS/NatCen report and its linked methodology were retrieved and reviewed for prevalence, isolation, family support, close friends, mental health, bullying, economic inactivity, in-person contact, organised activity and explicit non-causal limits; the report HTML page was hashed.
